source.title: CogBench: a large language model walks into a psychology lab
source.authors: Julian Coda-Forno; Marcel Binz; Jane X. Wang; Eric Schulz

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether model features, including parameter count and training-dataset size, predict performance on its cognitive benchmark. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss or reproduce the original scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports regression results for benchmark performance and model-basedness against model features. It does not report held-out cross-entropy losses, fits of loss power laws, compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or architecture-shape comparisons. The regression results about model-basedness are included as findings about scaling that do not match a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study is a cognitive-psychology benchmark. It does not reproduce scaling-law measurements. Its multilevel regression of average task performance on parameter count and training-token count across 35 LLMs is a new-setting result bearing on V6, because downstream performance rises with scale. It measures no pretraining loss, fits no power laws, and has no compute-optimal or shape analysis, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find parameter count significantly increases average performance and model-basedness, while dataset size and code data show no substantial effect. They rate Hypotheses 2 and 3 only 'partially supported'. They suggest data quality matters more than volume, and that size and data are confounded. They call the regression analysis preliminary and possibly imprecise because feature information on proprietary models is uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates behavioral and task-performance outcomes on CogBench rather than held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal training allocations.

fits_no_version.finding: Parameter count positively predicts model-basedness on the two-step task (β = 0.481). Dataset size and code fine-tuning do not significantly predict it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behavioural strategy metrics (e.g. model-based planning) shift with model size across LLMs, independently of training-token count.

fits_no_version.finding: Code fine-tuning has no substantial effect on average CogBench performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Code fine-tuning does not improve cognitive-task performance on CogBench.

record.problems: The authors say some proprietary model features are not transparent and that feature information was based on the best available knowledge, potentially affecting regression precision. They describe the analysis as preliminary. The relevant regression results concern cognitive benchmark outcomes, not held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported regression results omitted.

untested.parts: Whether improvement follows a predictable functional form (no curve fit or extrapolation). Performance as a function of pretraining loss. Within-family scaling isolated from data and fine-tuning differences. Conventional downstream suites.

missing.what: Per-task performance of the LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B base and chat models, a within-family size comparison holding data roughly fixed. It is shown only in figures, without numbers.
The parameter-count coefficients in the meta-cognition and risk-taking regressions are plotted but not reported in text. They are behavioural metrics, so likely none, but researchers may want them.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3. The paper is not aimed at the scaling question; it reports a cross-model regression in a new evaluation setting. Evidence for V6 is weak: there are 35 models from few families, many LLaMA-2 fine-tunes share size and data, some parameter counts are estimates (e.g. GPT-4 at 1760B), and the reported uncertainty for r1 is inconsistent.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests average performance on its cognitive benchmark against parameter count and training-dataset size, but not conventional downstream task suites or performance as a function of pretraining loss.

rows.subject: 35 LLMs (aggregate multilevel regression)
rows.size_stated: 35 LLMs; model parameter counts listed in billions in Appendix A
rows.operation_detail: Regressed average standardized performance across the benchmark tasks on model features, including number of parameters.

conditions.value: average standardized performance scores across all seven tasks

rows.note: The paper reports a significant positive effect of parameter count on average benchmark performance.
rows.check: Link and state are fine for direction only. This is a cross-family association with a positive coefficient, not a fitted scaling curve, so it does not show that the improvement is 'predictable'. The reported uncertainty (β = 0.277 ± 0.39 with z = 14.1) is internally inconsistent. The ± value may not be a standard error, so treat the uncertainty field with caution.

relationships.condition: Average standardized CogBench performance across 35 LLMs regressed on parameter count (multilevel model, family-nested)
relationships.reason: Parameter count has a significant positive coefficient on average performance (r1). This shows a monotone association, not a fitted law.
relationships.display_finding: Parameter count had a significant positive association with average performance across 35 models, without establishing a predictive scaling law.

relationships.condition: Same regression, training-dataset size as predictor
relationships.reason: Training-token count showed no substantial effect after controlling for parameters (r2). Collinearity with parameter count and imprecise dataset figures weaken this as evidence against data scaling.
relationships.display_finding: Training-token volume had no substantial effect after parameter adjustment, although collinearity and imprecise dataset estimates weakened the inference.
